title: Bayesian assessment of antarctic grounding line positions with sentinel-1 data and empirical priors
abstract: Bayesian updating provides a powerful route for quantifying uncertainty in geophysical inverse problems, such as the delineation of Antarctic grounding lines (GLs), which demarcate grounded from floating ice. GLs are required to calculate ice mass loss and consequently sea-level rise. However, most existing remote sensing based GL datasets lack spatially resolved positional uncertainty estimates. Hence, we developed an application agnostic Bayesian framework on top of the cross entropy based importance sampling for Bayesian updating (CEBU) algorithm to infer GLs from Sentinel-1 SAR range offsets over the Larsen C Ice Shelf by inverting a simple 1D elastic beam model. We explicitly propagate observational uncertainties through the likelihood and extend CEBU to incorporate empirical ice thickness information as a non-parametric prior. To diagnose convergence and parameter prioritization, we introduce the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, tracking information flow and enabling identification of non-informative updates. We further developed a data extraction approach that produces spatially dense quasi-1D profiles from 2D range offsets. The resulting GL estimates include full posterior probability density functions which were filtered based on thresholds derived using CEBU metrics. Because range offsets are less affected by interferometric decorrelation, the GLs are spatially and temporally dense. The most probable GL positions have mean and median distances of 361 m and 287 m from the 2019 manually delineated Sentinel-1 DInSAR lines. Our data extraction method also yielded more physically plausible posteriors in shear margin regions than the established flowline-based paradigm. The expert knowledge of ice thicknesses was propagated to other weakly constrained model parameters. This framework enables future development, including model evidence-based comparison of physical formulations, data extraction methods, applications to other ice shelves with challenging tidal or decorrelation conditions, and integration with more comprehensive rheological models. Together, these results highlight the potential of our Bayesian updating framework for a wide variety of large scale geophysical inverse problems.

title: Long-term limits on maximum ice sheet thickness around central Antarctic Peninsula nunataks
abstract: Understanding past ice sheet sensitivity to long-term climate cycles is essential to predict future sea-level rise. The Antarctic Peninsula Ice Sheet (APIS) is changing rapidly in one of Antarctica’s fastest warming regions. However, APIS thickness changes are poorly understood because there are limited terrestrial records of deglaciation. Here, the gap is filled by measuring cosmogenic nuclide ( 10 Be, 26 Al and 21 Ne) concentrations in 34 bedrock and boulder samples from high elevation nunataks in the APIS interior. Samples near the current ice surface record repeated burial by non-erosive ice mostly since ~890 ka. Nuclide ratios indicate that surfaces more than 121 – 170 m above current ice levels at Mount Faith, Mount Sullivan, and Engel Peaks have been ice-free for millions of years, reaching production-decay-erosion equilibrium with erosion rates as low as 0.14 ± 0.02 m Myr -1 . These limits contrast with numerical models which predict >250 m of thinning since the last glacial maximum, suggesting they are overestimating sea-level contribution from the central and eastern Antarctic Peninsula.

title: ISEFlow: a flow-based neural network emulator for improved sea level projections and uncertainty quantification
abstract: We developed ISEFlow, a new climate emulator model that predicts how melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica will contribute to future sea levels. It uses advanced machine learning to capture complex ice processes, distinguish between different emission scenarios, and provide clearer estimates of uncertainty. This makes sea level projections more accurate and reliable, helping scientists and policymakers better plan for climate risks.

title: Timing of Ocean–Atmosphere Variability and Its Impacts on Central Patagonian Ice Sheet Since MIS 3: Insights From Multiproxy Marine Records
abstract: Glaciers in southern mid‐latitudes during the late Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3) were likely strongly influenced by ocean‐atmosphere connections. However, the orbital‐ and millennial‐scale variability of the Patagonian Ice Sheet (PIS) remains poorly constrained, largely due to the scarcity of terrestrial records from the western Andean margin and the limited availability of continuous, well‐dated marine archives. Here, we present two continuous multiproxy marine records from the central Patagonian margin spanning the end of MIS 3 to the present. Site MD07‐3119 (46°S) is influenced by proximal ice‐sheet melting, whereas site MD07‐3082 (49°S) reflects the broader regional evolution of the PIS. Based on a new chronological approach, our data from the two cores constrain the last maximum extent of the central western PIS to ∼26.5(+0.83)–25.5(−0.52) ka, prior to the Last Glacial Maximum defined between 24.9–19.7 ka. Furthermore, high‐resolution ln(Ti/K) data and sediment accumulation rates reveal five millennial‐scale events of enhanced terrestrial sediment input, with increase factors of 1.6–30, coinciding with freshwater inputs and cooling of sea surface water and interpreted as central PIS advances and retreats. These millennial‐scale glacier fluctuations are synchronous with those reported for the New Zealand ice field, which may be explained by associated sea surface temperature changes and shifts of the Southern Westerly Winds, likely driven by climate variability in the South Pacific via ocean‐atmosphere interactions.

title: Basal sliding and ice rheology in West Antarctica constrained by multi-epoch satellite observations
abstract: A new method for the calibration of uncertain parameters in large-scale viscous ice-flow models is presented, with particular focus on the basal sliding law and ice rheology.The approach combines Bayesian inference with the rich information contained in successive satellite observations of ice-sheet elevation and velocity changes, and does not require knowledge of the surface or basal mass balance.The method is validated on a synthetic glacier with known physics, and subsequently applied to West Antarctica.The results support earlier evidence for a plastic basal rheology and strongly non-Newtonian creep within the regions ice streams.The stochastic framework provides a robust foundation for improved predictive simulations, offering data-driven constraints on how basal sliding and ice rheology may influence West Antarcticas future contribution to sea-level rise.

title: Greenland ice sheet retreat intensifies the African monsoon through a polar-tropical atmospheric teleconnection
abstract: Global climate forcing drives major changes in the North African summer monsoon (NASM), yet how high-latitude cryospheric changes influence tropical hydroclimate through atmospheric dynamics remains unclear. Integrating paleoclimate proxy evidence with coupled climate-model simulations, sensitivity experiments, and idealized atmospheric modeling, we show that Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) retreat acts as a dynamically important amplifier of NASM rainfall. Using the mid-Pliocene as a natural experiment for sustained global warming, we find that NASM rainfall was markedly stronger than that simulated under transient future warming for comparable global-mean temperature increases. GrIS retreat enhances Arctic warming, thereby perturbing the upper-tropospheric westerly jet and triggering a stationary Rossby wave train linking Greenland to North Africa. This polar–tropical atmospheric teleconnection strengthens monsoon circulation and moisture convergence, producing wetter conditions across the Sahara–Sahel. These results reveal a high-latitude pathway through which slow cryospheric changes modulate low-latitude monsoon variability under sustained warming.

title: Cyclical high-magnitude lake drainage slows Greenland ice sheet motion
abstract: Global glacier recession is driving a rapid increase in the number and volume of ice-marginal lakes, leading to more frequent Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). The long-term impact of GLOFs on glacier dynamics remains poorly understood, including in Greenland, which holds the largest glacial lake volume in the world. Here, using multi-decadal observations from Isortuarsuup Sermia, Southwest Greenland, we reveal that cyclical GLOFs regulate ice sheet motion. We identify a ‘sawtooth’ pattern of ice-dynamics, whereby multi-year acceleration is terminated abruptly by high-magnitude lake-drainage that resets the glacier to a ‘quiescent’ state for several years. The 2022 event exemplifies this process: the near-terminus ice velocity accelerated briefly from a pre-event baseline of ~200 m a −1 to ~1000 m a −1 before dropping to ~50 m a −1 over subsequent years. Each GLOF releases an immense meltwater volume (mean discharge in 2022 ~17000 m³ s −1), carving a ~1.5-km-wide, efficient subglacial channel. This channel enables extensive lowering of the subglacial water pressure, increasing ice–bed friction and suppressing ice motion. As climate warming increases GLOF frequency, this powerful negative feedback will modulate ice sheet motion acting as a brake on ice-dynamics at the margins of the Greenland Ice Sheet.

title: West Antarctic ice retreat temporarily halted with transient rheology in future climate projections
abstract: Sea level change and ice sheet stability depend on how Earth’s bedrock warps as ice melts. Rock experiments show that traditional models for bedrock deformation leave out important processes relevant for modern ice loss. We simulate the coevolution of the Antarctic ice sheet and global sea level under various climate change scenarios. When more realistic bedrock behavior is considered, Antarctic ice retreat is delayed. Ultimately, this has implications for larger Earth system feedbacks.

title: Mountain carbon budgets miss cryosphere hazard events
abstract: Warming is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere and triggering more frequent hazard events. These hazards mobilize large stores of carbon as well as rock, ice and water. Yet mountain carbon budgets largely overlook this flux, because routine monitoring rarely operates at the time, location and resolution that hazard events demand. We argue that cryosphere hazards should be treated as carbon events and set out how to close the gap. Here, cryosphere hazard events are mass movements in glacial and permafrost terrain whose onset is abrupt relative to gradual degradation, together with the cascades they trigger (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025). They range from rock-ice avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) lasting hours to retrogressive thaw slumps that develop within days to years as a form of abrupt thaw (Turetsky et al., 2020).At high elevations, warming is often amplified (Pepin et al., 2015(Pepin et al., , 2025)). Global glacier mass-loss rates rose by 36 ± 10% between 2000-2011and 2012-2023(Zemp et al., 2025)), and mountain permafrost is warming (Wu and Zhang, 2008;Noetzli et al., 2024) and thawing abruptly (Turetsky et al., 2020). GLOF frequency in the Third Pole has risen since 1980 (Zhang et al., 2023), and global GLOFs from moraine-dammed lakes increased from 5.2 to 15.2 per year between 1981-1990and 2011-2020(Zhang et al., 2025)). Retrogressive thaw slumps are spreading rapidly in alpine permafrost (Xia et al., 2024), driving cascading damage locally and downstream (Ding et al., 2021;Shugar et al., 2021). Existing frameworks recognize erosion, lateral transport, and outgassing as carbon pathways (Chapin et al., 2006;Hilton and West, 2020;Regnier et al., 2022), but lack a way to quantify hazard-driven mobilization and trace its fate (Figure 1a).A complete net ecosystem carbon budget needs vertical exchange from eddy covariance and chambers, and lateral export and outgassing from river and lake sampling (Chapin et al., 2006;Keenan and Williams, 2018), yet these observations rarely capture brief events or hillslope-channel transport.Three monitoring problems limit how cryosphere hazards enter carbon budgets. Temporal aliasing means periodic monitoring misses an event when the sampling interval exceeds a hazard-driven concentration peak. Extrapolation error means that, once a hazard resets sediment and carbon availability, pre-event concentration-discharge relationships no longer predict post-event fluxes. Material selectivity means that sampling of dissolved and suspended loads excludes carbon moved as woody debris, coarse bedload, or buried in deposits. No single method can constrain these fluxes: atmospheric observations cannot resolve lateral transfers, and satellite erosion detection cannot quantify the concentration or reactivity of displaced material. Figure 1. (a) Conceptual diagram showing cryosphere hazards-induced mobilization, transport, and transformation of carbon along a hazard-to-fate cascade. Cryosphere hazards, including glacier detachment, rock-ice avalanche, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) and thaw slump, connect mountain carbon stores to downstream environments. Cascading flows entrain carbon from soils, rock debris and vegetation, transporting it through channels to valley floors and receiving waters. Along these pathways, decomposition can release carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), whereas deposition and burial can retain carbon and vegetation recovery can restore CO2 uptake. Subsequent remobilization can expose stored material to further transport and decomposition, extending carbon effects beyond the initial disturbance. Whether a disturbance increases or decreases net carbon transfer to the atmosphere depends on carbon fate and ecosystem uptake, evaluated against a no-event trajectory over the same area and period. The diagram presents a conceptual accounting framework, not a quantified carbon budget, and unquantified pathways should not be read as zero fluxes. Over an accounting period, stock change within the boundary is ΔCstock = -Fatm -Fexport (Eq. 1), where Fatm is the cumulative net carbon flux to the atmosphere and Fexport is the net lateral export across the boundary, both positive when carbon leaves the system; burial within the boundary redistributes carbon within ΔCstock. POC, particulate organic carbon; DOC, dissolved organic carbon; DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon. (b) Gaps in representing cryosphere hazard events in mountain carbon budgets and ways forward.The consequence is systematic omission rather than random error. Hazard-driven fluxes are rare, brief and often occur in inaccessible terrain, so the disturbance-transfer term in the net ecosystem carbon balance usually lacks an empirical estimate and is underestimated. Known hazard fluxes come almost entirely from bespoke post-event surveys; after a GLOF, channelarmour disruption exposed sediment invisible to pre-event rating curves (Cook et al., 2018).The magnitude missed varies, so no single correction factor works across events. Earthquakeand storm-triggered landslides, used here as process analogues because their carbon export has been measured, show this variability. Landslide pulses increased biospheric carbon export (Hilton et al., 2008;Wang et al., 2016) and accounted for roughly 40% of organic carbon export in two New Zealand catchments (Howarth et al., 2025), whereas the Gorkha earthquake produced no detectable perturbation (Märki et al., 2021). Atmospheric inversions constrain aggregate CO2 exchange without attributing sources (Ciais et al., 2022), so a hazard signal may already sit within them unresolved.Cryosphere hazard cascades mobilize carbon spanning orders of magnitude in age and lability, from millennial permafrost organic matter and petrogenic rock carbon to recently fixed vegetation (Figure 1a). Source areas above treeline hold little biomass, but downstream cascades cross carbon-rich soils and forests. The 2023 South Lhonak disaster released about 50 million m 3 of water and eroded about 270 million m 3 of sediment (Sattar et al., 2025), yet its carbon was not estimated. A simple calculation shows the scale at stake. Assume a dry bulk density of 1.3-1.8 t/m 3 (Ji et al., 2020) and an organic carbon content of 0.43-0.79% for landslide debris from the Tibetan Plateau (Wang et al., 2023). The ~91 million m 3 of debris (excluding ice) detached at the China-Nepal border in 2026 (Li et al., 2026) would then hold roughly 0.51-1.29 Tg of organic carbon. That gross lateral mobilization is about 2.5-6.5 times the annual biospheric organic carbon export of the much larger Narayani catchment (Märki et al., 2021, their Fig. 4), mobilized in a few hours. This ratio is an upper bound, because the debris carbon also includes petrogenic carbon. Whether this carbon is flushed downstream, buried, or oxidized in the valley, it falls outside budgets built on routine river sampling.Mobilization changes the conditions that regulate decomposition. Aggregate disruption and exposure can increase microbial access, whereas mineral association and rapid burial may protect organic matter (Hilton and West, 2020). Carbon age alone does not determine lability.Old yet bioavailable dissolved organic matter occurs in Alaskan glacial runoff (Hood et al., 2009), and old carbon contributes substantially to river CO2 emissions (Dean et al., 2025). At permafrost thaw slumps, vegetation-free surfaces reduced respiration by about one-half but gross primary productivity by about four-fifths (Jiang et al., 2026a), and a plateau-wide synthesis found lower respiration in collapsed areas but increased CH4 release in alpine swamp meadows (Jia et al., 2026). Floods bury soil and biomass in valley fills, lakes and reservoirs, while channel reworking can later expose them. Drained thermokarst and proglacial lake beds and debris-flow surfaces are a particular blind spot, because dry inland waters can still emit carbon (Keller et al., 2020). The fate of mobilized carbon depends jointly on transport speed and reaction kinetics. Rapid flushing through cold, sediment-rich channels can export carbon before substantial mineralization, whereas retention in oxygenated sediments prolongs microbial breakdown.Hazards also mobilize inorganic carbon, exposing reactive minerals and changing waterrock interactions (Hawkings et al., 2026). Carbonic acid weathering and carbonation can consume CO2 (Styllas et al., 2026), whereas sulfide oxidation coupled to carbonate dissolution can release it (Hilton and West, 2020), and oxidation of petrogenic organic carbon is another CO2 source (Zondervan et al., 2023). In Tibetan Plateau rivers, net weathering is estimated to offset about 35% of river CO2 emissions (Zhang et al., 2026). Because hazard events mix inorganic and organic carbon, assessments based only on organic carbon decomposition may miss part of the response (Middelburg, 2024). The same mobilization couples carbon with other element cycles: permafrost thaw can increase N2O emissions (Voigt et al., 2020), glacial erosion exports reactive phosphorus (Hawkings et al., 2016), and thaw slumps release permafrost mercury, sharply raising methylmercury concentrations downstream (Schuster et al., 2018;St. Pierre et al., 2018).Whether a hazard event is a carbon source or sink depends on the quantity, boundary and processes assessed. Gross mobilization is the displacement of carbon from its original location, outlet export its transfer across a defined boundary, and net atmospheric exchange its transfer to or from the atmosphere. Redeposition within the same boundary redistributes carbon without creating a landscape sink, so these quantities should be accounted for separately and reconciled through mass balance (Eq. 1, Figure 1). We define the event term (Eq. 2, Figure 1) as cumulative net atmospheric carbon exchange with the event minus that under a specified no-event trajectory. Positive values indicate additional release or reduced uptake (a source), and negative values indicate additional uptake or avoided release (a sink). The reference site should share the affected site's warming and hydrology, differing only in the absence of the hazard. An event can thus increase atmospheric carbon relative to this reference while the landscape remains a net sink. Burial and ecological recovery can offset part of the disturbance, although forested-landslide evidence should be applied cautiously to alpine terrain. Post-Wenchuan sediment storage and revegetation raised carbon mass by about 10% (Liu et al., 2026), whereas greenness recovery after tundra thaw slumps took a decade at low-Arctic sites and more than 30 years at high-Arctic and highelevation sites (Xia et al., 2026). Greenness recovery does not imply recovered soil carbon stocks or net ecosystem exchange, so persistent productivity losses may matter even when deposited organic matter decomposes slowly.The atmospheric benefit of burial also depends on the reference trajectory. Relocating organic matter that would otherwise have remained protected adds little, whereas preserving material that would otherwise decompose avoids emissions (Galy et al., 2007). Only regrowth exceeding the no-event trajectory lowers the event term, and preserving petrogenic organic carbon averts a geological release without removing fixed atmospheric carbon. These distinctions keep sediment accumulation from supporting unwarranted sequestration claims.Field observations constrain exchange at some thaw slumps, geomorphic reconstructions constrain mobilization pathways, and downstream studies constrain delayed transport, yet few link all three within one event. Assessments should also report CO2-C and CH4-C separately, and converting CH4 emissions into a forcing metric requires an explicit metric and time horizon.We propose four priorities to close this gap (Figure 1b). First, establish a common accounting basis. Each assessment should specify its spatial boundary, accounting period, carbon forms and disturbance coverage, carry unsampled intervals into the uncertainty (Chapin et al., 2006;Ciais et al., 2022), and report mobilization, boundary export and the event term separately (Figure 1, Eqs. 1-2). This separates fluxes missing from an assessment from disturbance effects included but not attributed. Shared event identifiers should connect hazard inventories, water samples, deposit surveys and gas-flux records, distinguishing new erosion from remobilization of previously surveyed material (Jiang et al., 2026b).Second, trace carbon from source areas through transport pathways to deposits. Converting eroded volumes into carbon mass requires source material measurements that capture differences among lithologies, soil horizons, particle sizes and woody debris, with uncertainty in ice content and dry density propagated. Provenance measurements should distinguish biospheric from petrogenic carbon, because depleted radiocarbon alone cannot separate the two, and water chemistry should constrain weathering pathways and their CO2 uptake or release (Hilton and West, 2020). Post-event deposits record retained material but cannot reconstruct the dissolved and fine particulate carbon exported during the event (Märki et al., 2021).Third, connect short-lived transport pulses to longer-term carbon effects. Pre-positioned automatic samplers and redundant stream sensors can capture flood dynamics where deployment is safe (Cook et al., 2018). Later observations should track channel deposits, exposed lake beds, soil gas exchange and vegetation through successive seasons (Keller et al., 2020;Xia et al., 2026). Paired disturbed and reference sites separate event effects from regional change, and sediment cores can extend instrumental records if chronology and postdepositional carbon loss are treated explicitly (Howarth et al., 2025).Fourth, represent event diversity and overlapping legacies in regional models. Multiplying event frequency by a single mean carbon yield obscures differences among carbon-poor headwaters, vegetated valleys and efficient depositional traps. Models should link mobilization to carbon provenance, connectivity, transformation and ecological recovery, while allowing event recurrence to change and later floods to remobilize earlier deposits. Comparison with independent outlet fluxes or stock changes over a common period can show whether explicit event representation improves budget estimates.The approach generates testable expectations. Events crossing carbon-rich terrain with direct channel connections should mobilize more biospheric carbon than events confined to mineral debris (Hilton and West, 2020). Stable deposits should retain carbon longer than frequently reworked channels, and slow revegetation should prolong reductions in uptake.Testing these expectations would show where event accounting changes the inferred mountain carbon balance. Cryosphere hazards are becoming more frequent as warming continues (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025;Jiang et al., 2026b;Richter, 2026), so the carbon they mobilize is a growing budget term, and closing the observational gap is necessary to determine its climate feedback.

title: Progress in high-resolution paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental reconstructions at two Upper Pleistocene key localities in the loess type region of the Upper and Middle Rhine area (Germany)
abstract: In 1823/24 the term loess was introduced by Karl Caesar von Leonhard and its 200th anniversary was celebrated during the 2024 Loess Fest-conference in Mainz, Germany. Over these 200 years, loess research has evolved into a discipline of its own with initial approaches discussing the genesis and formation of this specific type of sediment, while later, the linkage to Quaternary climatic cycles was recognized. Nowadays, it is well known that loess–paleosol sequences (LPS) represent highly complex paleoclimatic and paleoenvironmental archives with great spatial extent in the terrestrial realm covering the entire Quaternary. Here we present the state of research for two LPS in von Leonhard’s eponym region that evolved to key sections for the last interglacial–glacial cycle during the last decades: Schwalbenberg in the Middle Rhine valley and Nussloch in the Upper Rhine area. We demonstrate that these sites contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling the interplay of sediment accumulation, soil formation, sediment relocation, and associated preservation of climate signals in LPS. Furthermore, methodological advances allow for reconstruction of paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic changes throughout the Upper Pleistocene on millennial- to centennial-scale resolution, highlighting the sensitivity of western European LPS to northern hemispheric climate oscillations.

title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.

title: An age calculator for high-latitude Quaternary foraminifera using amino acid racemization
abstract: Dating deep-sea cores from polar regions is challenging because sedimentation rates can be variable and oxygen-isotope stratigraphy can be ineffective, making amino acid racemization an important alternative. We calibrated the rate of racemization in Neogloboquadrina pachyderma , the dominant high-latitude planktic foraminifer, using 140 independently dated samples from 21 Arctic, Nordic Seas, North Atlantic, and Southern Ocean sites spanning 2 ka to 1.4 Ma. Racemization rates among these ocean basins differ less than among individual sites. Ages are based on aspartic acid, a more precise chronometer than glutamic acid, which, however, provides an independent check on the analysis. A publicly available age calculator returns formal uncertainty intervals incorporating calibration and measurement errors. Ages carry a realistic uncertainty of roughly ± 32% (66% level), insufficient to assign a sample to a specific Marine Isotope Stage but still useful for many polar marine sediment cores. A single age picks correctly between two candidate ages 90% of the time when they differ by a factor of 2.3 (e.g., 100 versus 230 ka). An independently dated horizon in the same core can reduce the uncertainty to ± 28%. Because comparisons are more precise than absolute ages, amino acid geochronology is best applied as a down-core series.

title: An accurate present-day model of the Antarctic ice sheet is necessary but insufficient for an accurate projection of its future evolution
abstract: Computer models of the Antarctic ice sheet can project how much it will melt in response to climate change. That depends on the properties of the rock and the water beneath the ice, about which we know very little. That means the amount of sea-level in the future is very uncertain. Techniques to reduce that uncertainty do not always work as well as expected. We must get actual measurements of the bottom of the ice to improve our understanding of the ice sheet, and our knowledge of its future.
authors: Roderik S. W. van de Wal

title: All-Weather Antarctic Ice Surface Temperature Retrieval from AMSR2 Using Machine Learning and Spatiotemporal Sampling Strategy
abstract: Ice surface temperature (IST) is a key variable for characterizing surface energy exchange and climate change over the Antarctic Ice Sheet. Thermal infrared (TIR) IST products provide high spatial resolution observations but suffer from substantial data gaps under cloudy conditions, whereas passive microwave (PMW) observations offer all-weather capability. However, retrieving IST from PMW observations remains challenging due to the complex interactions among microwave emission, snow and ice properties, atmospheric conditions, and surface temperature in polar regions. In this study, an all-weather IST retrieval framework was developed for the Antarctic Ice Sheet by integrating the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2) brightness temperatures with multi-source environmental variables using machine learning (ML) approaches. MODIS-derived IST estimates were used as reference observations, and a spatiotemporal sampling strategy was proposed to improve the representativeness of training samples under incomplete TIR observations. Three ML models, including Random Forest (RF), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were developed and evaluated. The results show that all three models successfully reproduced the spatial and seasonal variability of Antarctic IST, with lower uncertainties over the interior ice sheet and relatively higher uncertainties in coastal and ice-shelf margin regions. Among the three models, LightGBM performed most consistently, with RMSEs mainly ranging from 0.50 to 0.60 K relative to MODIS IST. Independent validation against automatic weather station (AWS) observations showed errors broadly comparable to those of MODIS IST, with clear-sky RMSEs of 2.37–5.26 K. The retrieved IST also exhibited consistent daily variations with MODIS observations in 2020, although generally higher temperatures were obtained, reflecting differences in the sensing mechanisms between microwave and TIR. The spatial pattern of the retrieved IST was physically consistent, characterized by the highest temperatures over the Antarctic Peninsula, intermediate temperatures in West Antarctica, and the lowest temperatures in East Antarctica. Overall, the proposed framework improves the spatiotemporal completeness of Antarctic IST observations while maintaining accuracy comparable to MODIS TIR products, supporting more continuous monitoring of Antarctic surface thermal processes and climate variability under all-weather conditions.

title: Evaluation of reanalysis datasets for studying high-elevation meteorological conditions in the Langtang Catchment, Nepal
abstract: Climate reanalysis datasets are widely used in hydro-meteorological and cryospheric research across High Mountain Asia (HMA), where in situ observations are scarce. Here, we evaluate ERA5L, High Asian Refined Analysis (HARv2), Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA2), and Climatologies at High Resolution for the Earth’s Land Surface Areas (CHELSA) against near-surface meteorological observations between 3,865 and 5,350 m a.s.l., in the upper Langtang Catchment, Nepal, using statistical metrics and Taylor Skill Score ( TSS ). We further assess their suitability for glacier surface energy balance (SEB) and mass balance modelling. No reanalysis product consistently outperforms the others; rather, their performance varies by meteorological variable, site, surface conditions, and timescale, with generally better performance at glacier sites, likely because their relatively homogeneous surface conditions are more readily represented by reanalysis products. Near-surface air temperature ( T 2m ) and humidity (specific: q and relative: RH ) are well reproduced ( TSS > 0.77) across products, although cold temperature and both dry and moist humidity biases are pervasive across sites. Wind speed ( u ) is poorly represented across products, sites, and timescales, reflecting their limited ability to resolve boundary layer processes and local katabatic and anabatic flows. Precipitation also exhibits large discrepancies, with ERA5L and HARv2 overestimating precipitation totals by ∼89–232% and MERRA2 and CHELSA underestimating by 30%–60%. They also generate frequent wet days and early-afternoon convective rainfall, in contrast to observed late-afternoon and nocturnal-to-early morning maxima. Hourly and daily SEB simulations at the Yala-on-Glacier site driven by reanalysis forcings yield statistically significant surface melt relative to reference estimates driven by in situ datasets; however, substantial differences in magnitude exist among products. ERA5L and HARv2 exhibit relatively small errors, largely due to compensating errors between radiative and turbulent fluxes, whereas MERRA2 and CHELSA show larger melt discrepancies due to their large radiative flux errors and underestimated precipitation that affects the surface albedo. Overall, our results underscore both the usefulness and limitations of reanalysis products for cryospheric applications in complex mountainous catchments and emphasize the need for assimilation of high-elevation observations in reanalysis products, alongside improved downscaling approaches, to better resolve local-scale atmospheric processes.

title: Drivers of reduced permafrost cooling efficacy of equatorial stratospheric aerosol injection in the Eastern Arctic compared to a moderate emission pathway
abstract: The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the world, causing permafrost – frozen ground – to thaw and release gases that accelerate climate change. Because emissions are not falling quickly enough, ways to cool the planet by reflecting sunlight back to space are being explored. Using climate model experiments, we study how this could affect permafrost. We find it could slow overall loss later this century, but shift thaw patterns, reducing it in some regions while increasing it in others.

title: A valley system investigation of Holocene coastal change and Irish Sea palaeogeography in Cardigan Bay, Wales, UK
abstract: Of the three substantial areas of postglacial aerial exposure on the Irish Sea shelf (Liverpool Bay, Cardigan Bay and the Bristol Channel), Cardigan Bay is the largest and the one about which we know the least. This article provides the first empirical sea level data for Cardigan Bay since the 1980s. It examines the proposition that the valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to a long period of marine influence that is not modelled in current palaeogeographical reconstructions. Detailed lithostratigraphic investigations traced the extent of Early to Mid‐Holocene marine influence in the Dysynni valley. Multiple microfossil proxies were used to calculate sea level data points. Two sea level index points from a back‐barrier marsh indicated relative sea level rise from −5.55 to −3.13 mOD between 7790–7630 and 6399–6296 cal. a BP. Freshwater/terrestrial limiting points from 7 km inland bracketed a period of marine influence between 9889–9545 and 4783–4416 cal. a BP. Pollen recorded a transition from saltmarsh, fen and reed‐swamp environments to alder carr and then birch woodland. The results were combined with existing lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data to show that the overdeepened glacial valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to marine influence from before 12 000 cal. a BP, with different palaeogeographical histories dependent on their depths and rates of postglacial sedimentation.

title: Climate-related signals in the GV7-C ice core from East Antarctica for 1782–2013 CE: potential relevance to climate and teleconnections between the tropics and Antarctica
abstract: This research explores climate patterns recorded in Antarctic ice over the past two centuries. By analyzing ice layers, we identified connections between Antarctica's climate and tropical ocean conditions. Results show changing influences over time and highlight the Indian Ocean's key role in Antarctic snowfall. This improves understanding of how polar and tropical climates interact, crucial for future climate predictions.

title: Post-depositional processes affecting water stable isotope records at Little Dome C, Antarctica: new records from two firn cores and virtual firn core modelling
abstract: This study presents the water isotope profiles of two firn cores drilled at Little Dome C (LDC) in Antarctica and dated by identifying volcanic events, which enabled us to determine an accumulation rate at LDC of 24 mmwe.yr-1. Comparison of a virtual firn core model with these data allowed us to study the surface processes responsible for isotopic variability in firn. We therefore suggest that future models consider the mixing of the surface layer and re-quantify diffusion.

title: Reconstructing Ross Sea cryosphere–ocean variability during the Miocene Climatic Optimum using palynology
abstract: The fate of the Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) under climate warming remains highly debated. Geological evidence from the warm Miocene Climatic Optimum (MCO, ∼ 17–14.7 Ma) is still limited to a few circum-Antarctic records but generally suggests substantial AIS retreat and reduced or absent sea ice. Yet the magnitude and temporal variability of the cryosphere dynamics within the generally warm MCO remain poorly constrained. Here, we present a marine and terrestrial palynological record from sediments recovered at site U1521 on the outer shelf of the central Ross Sea during the International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 374, spanning portions of the interval ∼ 17.3–14.5 Ma. Dinoflagellate cysts and freshwater-tolerant and brackish-water algae indicate variable surface ocean temperature, productivity and ice melting related to the transition from a marine-terminated ice sheet (16.3–16.2 Ma) to fully open-ocean peak warmth conditions (16.0 Ma). Terrestrial palynomorphs also indicate alternate cooling and warming phases on the hinterland, closely coupled to ice and ocean dynamics. Persistent vegetation implies continued (at least partially) ice-free terrestrial habitats. These results highlight substantial variability in AIS and ocean conditions during the MCO despite an overall warm climate state.

title: Spatial Shift in Southern Ocean Seasonal Ice Zone Production Trends
abstract: In recent decades, satellite observations have reported a marked increase in primary production across the Seasonal Ice Zone (SIZ) of the Southern Ocean, indicating enhanced ecosystem activity and a potential rise in biological carbon storage. However, the spatial coherence and temporal stability of these trends remain poorly constrained. Here, using satellite observations and model-based data from 1998/99 to 2023/24, we detect two successive regime shifts in austral summer SIZ primary production. The first, around 2007/08, marks a transition from a dipole—characterized by declining production in the Weddell Sea and increasing production in the Amundsen Sea—to a basin-wide increase across the SIZ. The second, around 2014/15, represents an intensification of this basin-wide pattern under accelerated sea-ice loss. Mechanistically, the initial 2007/08 structural shift is likely triggered by the reversal of the Southern Annular Mode (SAM), which restructured regional sea-ice distribution via rapid Ekman-driven atmospheric forcing. For the post-2007/08 period, sea-ice redistribution fundamentally altered light penetration, while wind-driven mixed-layer shoaling further enhanced light availability, promoting a widespread rebound in primary production. In contrast, the slow response to persistent SAM forcing—via enhanced Circumpolar Deep Water upwelling—progressively decreased sea-ice concentration, reaching a critical tipping point around 2014/15 that accelerated the basin-wide sea-ice decline. For the post-2014/15 period, the accelerated sea-ice loss directly reduced surface albedo and introduced substantial meltwater, which further shoaled the mixed layer, collectively driving a stronger productivity increase. These results have implications for projecting future changes in regional primary production and assessing the broader impacts on the Southern Ocean's biological carbon pump.

title: Snow Phenology over Antarctic Sea Ice and Its Lagged Relationship with Sea Ice Thickness
journal: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
abstract: Snow over Antarctic sea ice influences surface energy exchange, sea-ice growth, and surface mass balance, yet its seasonal evolution remains poorly understood due to sparse observations and uncertainties among retrieval methods. The timing of Antarctic sea-ice transitions has also exhibited substantial regional variability, raising the need to understand how snow phenology evolves with sea-ice conditions. Here, monthly snow-depth reconstructions from three deep-learning frameworks, including a convolutional neural network (CNN), the Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN), and multilayer perceptron (MLP), are used to characterize Antarctic snow phenology, including snow-onset month, snow-melt month, snow-season length, and annual maximum snow depth. Spatial trends of phenological metrics are quantified, and lagged relationships between snow depth and sea-ice thickness (SIT) are examined across 0–5 month lags. All three reconstruction frameworks reproduce the dominant seasonal cycle of Antarctic snow depth, characterized by reduced accumulation during austral summer and enhanced accumulation during winter and spring. The derived phenological metrics exhibit pronounced regional variability, with model differences most evident in snow-melt timing and snow-season length. Trend patterns reveal spatially heterogeneous changes rather than a uniform circumpolar response. Correlations between monthly snow-depth and SIT anomalies are strongest at short lags and decrease with increasing temporal offsets, showing that their monthly departures are most closely aligned over short intervals. The spread among reconstructions highlights the influence of model-dependent uncertainty on derived snow-phenology indicators and emphasizes the importance of multi-model assessments for interpreting Antarctic snow–ice coupling.

title: A record of polyphase Middle Pleistocene glaciation in the Sudetic Foreland, SW Poland
abstract: The Sudetic Foreland of Central Europe preserves an important sedimentary archive for reconstructing Pleistocene dynamics of the Scandinavian Ice Sheet, although the timing and character of pre-Saalian glaciations remain poorly constrained. This study presents an integrated sedimentological, structural, petrographic, and geochronological investigation of glaciogenic deposits exposed at the Jaźwina gravel pit. Two litho-petrographically distinct till units (T1 and T2) record changes in sediment provenance linked to the South Polish Complex (Elsterian1/2; MIS12/16). Glaciotectonic mesostructures indicate deformation under WNW–ESE-directed compression, interpreted as the combined effect of ice loading and reactivation of the Sudetic Marginal Fault. 10 Be– 26 Al burial dating of Fennoscandian erratics from the lower T1 till constrains its maximum depositional age to 620 ± 480 ka. Macrofossil wood remains (Quercus sp., Abies sp.) beneath the glacial succession are interpreted as redeposited from Early Pleistocene fluvial sediments. The combination of deformed tills, variable provenance signatures, and overprinted ice-flow indicators supports a polyphase glacial history involving thrust stacking of Middle Pleistocene deposits and subsequent tectonically driven denudation of the uppermost MIS 6 (Uciechów) till. These findings provide the first direct cosmogenic-nuclide age constraints for Middle Pleistocene tills and underscore the value of site-specific studies for resolving pre-Saalian glacial chronologies in Central Europe.

title: Bioclimatic and habitat signals in Pleistocene fluvial microvertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine
abstract: Fluvial microvertebrate assemblages are important but underexplored archives for reconstructing Quaternary environments, particularly in regions lacking karstic and cave deposits. We analyse late Middle and early Late Pleistocene small‐vertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine, to compare two interpretative frameworks: habitat‐weighting analysis and bioclimatic spectra. The studied assemblages span multiple Marine Isotope Stages (MIS 11 to MIS 5) and derive exclusively from alluvial contexts characterised by taphonomic overprinting and time‐averaging. Using principal component analysis, we compare the environmental signals extracted by both methods across different taxonomic datasets. In both approaches, the dominant source of variation reflects changes in ecological evenness, expressed as shifts in the relative importance of steppe, tundra–steppe and high‐latitude taxa. The most even assemblages correspond to cold‐stage conditions and are characterised by arctic and boreal elements, whereas low‐evenness assemblages are dominated by core tundra–steppe taxa. Habitat spectra additionally capture geomorphological influences related to river‐valley dynamics, resulting in a diffuse climatic signal. In contrast, bioclimatic spectra more directly resolve glacial–interglacial climatic gradients and show greater robustness to incomplete faunal lists and taphonomic biases. Our results demonstrate that bioclimatic spectra provide a clearer palaeoclimatic signal than habitat‐based approaches for fluvial microvertebrate assemblages. This method is therefore particularly well suited to Quaternary environmental reconstruction in lowland river systems affected by taphonomic and sedimentary filtering.

title: Last glacial North Pacific oxygenation due to North Atlantic circulation changes
abstract: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02122-x Transient weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation during the last glacial period may have led to a contraction of oxygen minimum zones in the North Pacific, according to benthic foraminifera proxy records and Earth system simulations.

title: A small ensemble of bias-adjusted CMIP6 climate simulations over North America extending to 2300
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Even if many sectors would benefit from scientific evidence on the long-term consequences of current policy choices, most climate projections end in 2100. This paper describes a collection of bias-adjusted climate simulations extending to 2300. It includes few Earth System Models, most of them driven by scenarios at the very low or very high end of the range of plausible futures. The composition of the ensemble makes it difficult to deliver climate services supporting climate risk assessments.

title: Exchange between ocean and Greenland fjords regulated by recirculating meltwater in glacial troughs
abstract: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02147-2 The recirculation of glacial meltwater within a deep Greenland fjord inhibits the inflow of relatively warm ocean water, slowing further glacial melt, according to hydrographic observations and numerical modelling.

title: Basin-Scale Nonlinear Dynamics of Thermohaline Ocean Circulation. Part I: Theory
abstract: arXiv:2611.33383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Earth's thermohaline ocean circulation may support multiple equilibria and abrupt transitions. Similar bifurcation structures for different ocean models suggest common underlying dynamics across the model hierarchy. Here we propose a unifying framework from tracer conservation, in which surface fluxes are balanced by dissipative and advective tracer transport. We express this flux balance through a large-scale tracer gradient and a transport efficiency that measures how strongly circulation displaces the tracer field from its no-flow "conductive" state. The flux balance quantifies the transport contributions that sustain each circulation state and give rise to abrupt transitions. In a three-dimensional ocean-basin model, we find nonlinear salinity advection dominates the collapse threshold and linear dissipation dominates the recovery threshold. Temperature has additional dissipation from surface restoring, making thermal fluxes more dissipation-dominated than salinity fluxes. The tracer contrasts and boundary layers that a given circulation generates produce distinct transport regimes, approximately quadratic in circulation strength for weak flow and linear for strong flow. With a simple circulation closure, the flux balance reduces to longstanding box-model bifurcation results for the weak and strong flow regimes. Thus, by expressing thermohaline bifurcations through basin-scale transport, this framework connects box-model insight to the continuous equations. Furthermore, as this framework exposes the transport processes that balance a changing forcing, it provides constraints on a thermohaline ocean state and its trend toward tipping that overturning strength alone does not. In Part II, we develop flux-balance closures to forecast such tipping points.

title: Joint Bayesian calibration of frontal ablation and climatic mass balance in global glacier models (PyGEM-OGGM-SERMeQ v1.0)
abstract: We present a new framework to model frontal ablation of marine-terminating glaciers by linking two global glacier models with a simple physics-based calving scheme and Bayesian calibration. Applied to 71 Svalbard glaciers (2000–2019) and projected to 2100, it reproduces seasonal front changes but overestimates ablation due to uncertain geometry and velocity. This efficient approach can improve regional to global simulations.

title: Sub-regional warming, cryosphere change, and climate vulnerability hotspots in Pakistan's HKH region: Insights from CMIP6 projections and remote sensing

title: Attribution of climate extremes with global temperature regressions: accounting for uncertainty from internal variability
abstract: Attribution of climate change to anthropogenic forcing is an important goal in climate science. Regression of local conditions on global temperatures is a popular statistical approach, but whether the uncertainty derived from observations alone can reflect the range of outcomes possible due to internal variability remains unclear. Here, we use large ensembles from three climate models as an idealized testbed to quantify the role of internal variability for such attribution of climate extremes with single climate realisations. Internal variability generates large uncertainty in the linear-regression slope between global temperatures and regional temperature extremes, exceeding 40% of the ensemble mean slope across 50, 38, and 9% of the global surface area in the MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR and CanESM5 models respectively. Nevertheless, we show that these uncertainties can be accurately inferred from individual ensemble members using a block-bootstrap procedure - offering potential for a robust application to observations. Block-bootstrapping also accurately captures the absolute uncertainty for precipitation extremes, despite a substantially smaller signal-to-noise ratio which leads to underestimated and overly noisy estimates of relative uncertainty at present-day warming levels. This work provides a basis for the attribution of climate extremes from observations which can robustly capture the uncertainty associated with internal climate variability.

title: Estimating the impact of ice-sheet surface height and ice-divide variability on ice-core based climate reconstructions
abstract: Ice drilled from deep inside Antarctica reveals how climate changed over hundreds of thousands of years. However, the ice sheet itself rises and sinks over time, which can distort temperatures read from the ice. Using three computer simulations covering the last two million years, we show that drilling sites rose and sank by up to 240 metres and their summits shifted by up to 120 kilometres, and we estimate how this biases climate records, including potential for the oldest ice.

title: Alternate states and intermingledness in complex high-dimensional systems
abstract: by George Datseris, Johannes Lohmann, Oisín Hamilton, Jacob Haqq-Misra Many natural systems posses, and can transition between, multiple alternative states. For example, a climate “tipping element” is a climate component that can transition to an alternative steady state due to an external perturbation such as global warming. Despite the potential impact, existence of alternate states in realistic, complex simulations (e.g., climate models) remain poorly understood. Arguably a reason for this is the lack of applicable methodology that explicitly targets finite yet high-dimensional datasets. In this work we utilize recent progress in computational nonlinear dynamics to formulate a workflow that analyses potentially multi-state simulation data and decides algorithmically what are the alternate states contained within, if any are clearly distinguishable. The framework undergoes an optimization routine that showcases which observables in the data best differentiate the alternate states, and which ones do not differentiate at all, which could be used to guide monitoring and early-warning for multistable components in climate or ecosystems. Finally, once the alternate states have been found, we define an indicator called “intermingledness”. It quantifies differences and similarities between alternate states, as well as for their basins of attraction (if applicable), across various diagnostic variables. We analyse and present results using three diverse climate datasets: Atlantic ocean circulation, atmospheric midlatitude flow, and habitability of exoplanets. The method is not exclusive to climatic data, but applicable to a variety of cases characterised by high dimensional data and presence of alternate states, including complex networks such as power grids or biological networks. We also provide easy-to-use open source code for applying the workflow to new data.

title: Estimating Ocean Heat Content from Satellite Altimetry, Space Gravimetry, and In Situ Observations closes the Earth’s Energy Budget on Interannual to Decadal Time-scales
abstract: The ocean stores more than 90% of the excess energy associated with Earth’s radiative imbalance (EEI), making accurate ocean heat content (OHC) estimates essential for closing the global energy budget. We introduce MOHeaCANv6, a new global OHC reconstruction for 2004–2023 that combines satellite altimetry, space gravimetry, and in-situ Argo observations within a unified inverse framework. Satellite-derived thermosteric sea level provides a physically-based prior, locally calibrated to Argo OHC using least squares, followed by objective mapping of residuals to recover unresolved variability. This approach exploits the global coverage and continuity of satellites while retaining Argo’s in-situ accuracy. MOHeaCANv6 provides spatially and temporally consistent OHC estimates for 0–1000m, extended to full depth using satellite constraints on vertically integrated OHC. Cross-validation against withheld Argo profiles indicates local errors generally below 10%(2σ) of the signal. Globally, OHC increases at 9.8±2.1ZJyr −1 (2σ), corresponding to a mean ocean heat uptake (OHU) of 0.81±0.23Wm −2 (2σ) over 2004–2023, with an OHU trend of 0.58±0.4Wm −2 dec −1 (2σ) over 2005–2022. A key result is the close agreement between OHU and an independent estimate derived from CERES top-of-atmosphere radiation combined with ERA5 atmospheric energy divergence and storage over the ocean. The annual time series correlate at 0.88, and the global energy budget is closed within ±0.5Wm −2 on interannual time scales. This unprecedented level of precision in the closure paves the way for detecting and tracking, within the energy budget, the excess energy entering the system due to the positive, time-averaged EEI of ~1 W.m −2. This closure also confirms the robustness of the observed 0.47±0.4Wm −2 dec −1 increase in Earth’s energy imbalance by CERES and demonstrates that the vast majority of excess energy is stored in the ocean including the excess energy coming from the radiative imbalance over land.

title: Future meltwater dynamics and water balance components under climate warming and land use change in a cryosphere-dominated basin of the Tibetan plateau
Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
abstract: arXiv:2611.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

title: Glacier Albedo Variability During Transportation Infrastructure Construction: A Case Study of the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel
abstract: Glacier surface albedo influences melt and may respond to climatic variability, changing surface conditions, and particulate emissions from nearby infrastructure. This study examined albedo variability across 434 glaciers near the Tianshan Shengli Tunnel during 2018–2024 using MODIS MOD10A1, Landsat 8/9 observations, ERA5 winds, and excavation records. Mean albedo during 2020–2024 was lower than during 2018–2019 by 0.025 for MODIS and 0.032 for Landsat. A distinct MODIS pixel-level quality-screening comparison applying an 80% daily valid-area coverage threshold yielded a descriptive difference of −0.0278. In the matched 357-glacier August–September sample, trends were −0.00597 yr−1 for the original masks and −0.00615 yr−1 after 60 m inward buffering; both 95% confidence intervals included zero. Cross-sensor observations covaried strongly (r = 0.867), although the bias of −0.073 and RMSE of 0.086 indicated substantial disagreement in magnitude. The climate-adjusted MODIS post-2020 coefficient was non-significant (−0.0190; p = 0.287), while the Landsat coefficient changed sign with trend specification. Across six excavation intervals, the construction-activity proxy showed a non-significant association with albedo anomalies (Spearman ρ = −0.543; exact p = 0.297), with direction sensitive to the reference baseline. Seasonal wind alignment described regional directional relationships but did not establish particle transport or deposition. The observations document lower later-period albedo and a negative interior-mask trend tendency without isolating a construction contribution. These findings support continuous dust control during emission-generating activities and coordinated glacier, meteorological, and deposition monitoring.

title: Distinguishing dynamic and thermal effects of the Tibetan Plateau on the Asian dust cycle using regional climate modeling
abstract: The Tibetan Plateau (TP) has profound influence on the Asian dust cycle through dynamic and thermal effects, yet quantification of the impacts of these effects remains inadequate. This study employed the Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) to systematically quantify the impacts of the two effects of the TP on dust cycle across six major Asian deserts through numerical experiments. The simulated results revealed that the dynamic effect suppresses springtime dust emission in the Taklimakan Desert by more than 500 mg m −2 day −1 but enhances that considerably (by almost 300–500 mg m −2 day −1) over the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect intensifies summer dust activity in the Thar Desert (by 500 mg m −2 day −1) and the Qaidam Basin, and is closely linked to strong convection and monsoon flows. The dust loading of East Asia peaks in spring under the dominance of the dynamic effect of the TP, while that in South Asia peaks in summer, driven primarily by the thermal effect of the TP. The dust deposition patterns indicate that the dynamic effect inhibits dust accumulation in the Taklimakan Desert, but promotes deposition on the Loess Plateau. The thermal effect enhances dust deposition through monsoon-related changes in soil moisture. The dynamic effect alters near-surface winds via topographic channeling and jet stream bifurcation, while the thermal effect modulates boundary layer stability and the large-scale circulations. This quantitative study elucidated how the dual forcings of the TP dynamically shape the patterns of the Asian dust cycle, providing critical constraints for Earth System Models.

title: A comprehensive global ocean radiocarbon  dataset (1700–2024) for climate applications
abstract: Radiocarbon measurements in the ocean are key to studying ocean circulation, gas exchange and the carbon cycle, but they are sparse and scattered across many sources. We combined about 68,500 measurements from ship-based seawater samples (1955–2024) and biogenic carbonates (corals and shells, 1700–2020) into one quality-checked, openly available dataset. The dataset provides the most comprehensive record of ocean radiocarbon over the industrial period, including impacts of nuclear bomb tests.

title: Fidelity and stratigraphy of the Antarctic Allan Hills old ice archive from continuous flow analysis
abstract: The Allan Hills contains the oldest known ice, extending records millions of years. However, this area along the Transantarctic Mountains margin results in stratigraphically discontinuous ice core records. Here, we investigate high-resolution geochemical records to better constrain biases and stratigraphic complexities, and find these records exhibit reduced variance, some degree of interglacial bias, with varying behaviours across ice cores at the Allan Hills.

title: Observationally-constrained CMIP6 projections of a snow-free Northern Hemisphere
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79797-8 This study presents a monthly emergent constraint based on observed warming that reduces CMIP6 inter-model variance and refines snow-free projections: Arctic summers become snow-free by 2040 s under SSP5-8.5, while snow disappearance is delayed by 7–34 years under SSP1-2.6 in vulnerable regions and months.

title: Boron isotopes in fluvial palaeochannels reveal catchment weathering and climate variability over the last glacial–interglacial cycle
abstract: Boron (B) isotopes in fluvial clay fractions can provide information about catchment weathering and vegetation–soil interactions during past environmental change. We investigate clay- and sand-fraction B isotope compositions, clay B/Al ratios, mineralogy and neodymium isotopes from 14 sites across four Murrumbidgee River palaeochannel systems in southeastern Australia, spanning the last glacial–interglacial cycle. Sampling position, mineralogical assemblages and geochemical observations are combined to assess potential post-depositional overprinting. Several shallow or exposed samples have elevated δ 11 B, consistent with interaction with isotopically heavy soil or pore waters. In the screened dataset, clay–sand isotope offsets (Δ 11 Bclay–sand) are relatively low in Yanco and Gum Creek sediments and more positive in Kerarbury, Coleambally and recent deposits. Overlapping εNd compositions provide no clear evidence for a systematic provenance shift among systems. The boron isotope contrasts, considered alongside regional vegetation records and clay mineralogy, suggest changes in the influence of biologically modified soil solutions on catchment weathering products. More positive offsets are consistent with greater vegetation-mediated B cycling, whereas lower offsets in the younger systems may reflect reduced biological processing, increased contributions from deeper regolith, or both. Published palaeohydrological evidence places these younger deposits within periods of enhanced fluvial activity, suggesting that greater water and sediment delivery coexisted with a reduced biological imprint on exported clays. The results demonstrate the potential of boron isotopes to complement fluvial and vegetation archives by tracing changes in catchment weathering regime, while emphasising the importance of assessing post-depositional preservation.

title: OMNIE-Nutrients: A Global Gridded Ocean Nutrient Dataset (1965–2022) Derived from a Neural Network Emulator and In-Situ Observations
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) OMNIE-Nutrients is a global gridded dataset of marine macronutrients (nitrate, phosphate, silicate) spanning 1965–2022. It integrates sparse in situ observations with machine-learning-emulated profiles derived from hydrographic data, expanding the effective observational network by an order of magnitude. These interpolated fields eliminate severe artifacts and historical sampling biases prevalent in standard climatologies, providing a robust baseline for evaluating biogeochemical variability.

title: Structurally preconditioned continental-shelf troughs define potential warm-water pathways in Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica
abstract: We present new shipboard bathymetry from Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica, acquired during three summers with reduced fast-ice cover to resolve glacier-front bathymetry and assess its relationship to inherited crustal structure and potential warm-water access. Echo-soundings in front of glacier systems reveal a network of deep troughs and shallow sills across the inner continental shelf. The Shirase Glacier system is connected to the deeper continental shelf through an entrance approximately 740 m deep, whereas shallower sills of approximately 480–580 m occur at the entrances to the Skallen, Telen, and Honnør glacier-front troughs. These depth contrasts define bathymetric thresholds that may modulate warm-water access under varying oceanographic conditions. The NW–SE-trending segment of the main trough is spatially aligned with a structural lineament inferred from a major airborne magnetic-anomaly boundary, suggesting that inherited basement structure may have influenced the localization of glacial erosion. Together, these observations suggest that inherited basement structure may have helped shape a segmented trough-and-sill morphology that now provides potential pathways and bathymetric thresholds for warm-water access, offering a geological framework for interpreting modern and Holocene ice–ocean interactions in Lützow-Holm Bay.

title: Spatial structure of diatom communities inhabiting Antarctic cryoconite holes
abstract: Cryoconite holes are water-filled depressions on glacier surfaces hosting a broad range of organisms, including diatoms. Yet, the biogeographic structure of these diatom communities has not been explored for the Antarctic Realm. Combining both light microscopy and rbcL metabarcoding, we investigated spatial variation in cryoconite diatom communities across two major Antarctic regions (i.e. Antarctic Peninsula and Continent), each represented by four additional subregions. Well-developed diatom communities were observed in most subregions, with species and genus richness comparable across sites, and molecular results generally in agreement with morphological observations at the genus level. A small number of taxa dominated, with six genera accounting for ~95% of all valves counted. Of these, Psammothidium and Humidophila were the most abundant and prevalent, while the genus Muelleria was common in, yet confined to, one subregion (McMurdo Dry Valleys). Beta-diversity analyses revealed clear differences in diatom community composition among regions and subregions. Notably, ~87% of all species were region-specific (81% on the Peninsula and 73% on the Continent), indicating pronounced spatial structure. Accordingly, our results suggest that the integration of dispersal limitation, environmental characteristics, and regional history influences cryoconite diatom community assembly at large spatial scales, and advance our understanding of microbial ecology within Antarctica.

title: Orbital forcing of sedimentation and deep-water circulation changes in Doldrums Fracture Zone, Central Atlantic, over the last 260 kyr
Diagnosing the Roles of Large-Scale Circulation in Tropical Precipitation Biases in CESM2 Using Nudging Technique
abstract: Persistent tropical precipitation biases in general circulation models can arise from errors in both the large-scale environment and the subgrid-scale processes that produce precipitation, making their respective contributions difficult to isolate. Here, we evaluate precipitation in the Community Earth System Model version 2.2.2 (CESM2) using a revised nudging framework that constrains horizontal winds, specific humidity, and/or temperature toward reanalysis. Constraining horizontal winds substantially reduces climatological precipitation biases across the tropical Pacific, including dry biases over the western Pacific warm pool and northern Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and wet biases in the subtropics. Importantly, replacing the largescale circulation with reanalysis also shifts precipitation from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities, despite no modifications to the model’s moist physics parameterizations. This improvement is closely associated with reorganized moisture transport and more frequent strong moisture convergence events, even in regions where the climatological humidity does not increase. Further constraining specific humidity or temperature provides no systematic additional improvement, highlighting the central role of circulation in setting the environment to which moist physics parameterizations respond. However, regional biases remain, particularly an underestimation of heavy precipitation, even though model’s lower troposphere remains closer to saturation than in reanalysis during substantial precipitation events. Together, the substantial shift from overly frequent light rainfall toward heavier intensities under circulation constraint indicates that errors in the large-scale environment contribute importantly to precipitation biases in CESM2, while the remaining discrepancies likely also reflect limitations in the moist physics parameterizations.

title: An open-source tool for mapping key metrics of glacier health from space
abstract: Satellite-based observations enable monitoring of glacier health metrics, essential for assessing glacier response to climate change and the environmental services they provide. Here, we present a Google Earth Engine tool for automated mapping of key climate- and mass balance- modulated parameters, including total visible ice area, snow-covered area (SCA), accumulation-area ratio, and snowline altitude (often used as a proxy for the equilibrium-line altitude). The tool uses Landsat near-infrared reflectance, commonly used spectral band ratios, and scene-specific thresholding to distinguish snow-covered from ice or firn surfaces. Validation for 60 glaciers across 13 regions shows strong agreement with manual observations of satellite imagery and weaker agreement with field-based observations from the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS), likely reflecting differences in methodology and observation timing. The tool substantially improves WGMS temporal coverage, filling ~63% of glacier-year gaps and increasing the total number of observations (e.g., SCA by ~65%). Beyond the glaciers studied here, the tool is designed to enable efficient and accessible generation of multi-decadal glacier health time series for individual glaciers globally, with appropriate user evaluation and consideration of known limitations. Thus, the tool will hold value for a range of academic and non-academic users, particularly for education, outreach, and community stakeholders.

title: Sea-level and monsoon precipitation controls on sedimentary organic carbon burial on the northern South China Sea continental shelf during the early Holocene
Quantifying the role of temporal-scale-dependent precipitation change in mass balance in the Dongkemadi Glacier, Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Understanding how precipitation changes affect glaciers is critical for predicting their future responses as well as for forecasting water supplies and potential impacts on downstream lowland regions. This study evaluated the effects of precipitation changes at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales on the mass balance of the Dongkemadi (DKMD) Glacier (central Tibetan Plateau) during 1960–2009. Results showed increasing trends in precipitation at the annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, except in July (decreasing trend). Warm season (i.e., the glacier’s melt season) precipitation constituted 91.4% of annual precipitation, and accounted for 80.3% of the annual precipitation increase. A comparison of precipitation changes effects across the three scales revealed: i) All three precipitation trends increased annual, warm season and monthly glacier mass balance, except in July; ii) Using monthly precipitation trends captured the monthly variability of precipitation-induced mass balance changes (range: 50 mm w.e.); iii) Annual or seasonal precipitation trends underestimated mass balance changes by approximately 22%; iv) The direct driver of mass balance increase was enhanced mass inputs (i.e., snowfall) from increased precipitation, which accounted for over half of the total increase in mass balance; and v) The indirect driver was reduced melt energy, primarily attributed to decreased net shortwave radiation caused by higher surface albedo. This study confirms the effectiveness of using monthly precipitation trends to investigate how precipitation changes impacted on the DKMD Glacier and its meltwater runoff. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for accurately assessing precipitation changes effects on the energy and mass balance of glaciers globally.

title: Combining geodetic data and summer MODIS albedo anomalies for annual glacier mass balance estimation
abstract: We introduce a new satellite-based approach to estimate annual glacier mass balance. Comparison with extensive field measurements shows strong agreement, demonstrating that this method can reliably track annual glacier changes across large regions.
